questions.ask: What should the audience think, feel or do differently after this deck?
options: Change how they understand a situation
Feel ready and motivated to act
Leave with a concrete next step

questions.ask: Who is the audience, what do they already know, and what do they care about?
options: Decision makers: short on time, focused on cost and risk
A technical team: wants depth and evidence
A mixed room: needs both the overview and the detail

questions.ask: If they remember one thing, what is it? Complete the sentence: after this deck, my audience will know, believe or do ...
How should the argument be structured?
options: A ranked or themed list of points

questions.ask: What data, examples or demos can support the message?
options: Reports or documents to draw from
Nothing yet: the deck marks where evidence will go

questions.ask: Which language is the deck in? It also sets the date format.
How long is it: a number of slides, or a time budget?
Is it speaker-led, with few words and large visuals, or a reading deck that must stand on its own?
Which of the brand's themes should lead? Backgrounds can be mixed slide by slide.
Which classification label goes on the slides?
Should every slide carry a short header? Leave it empty for none.

steps.title: Slide outline
steps.what: Write a slide-by-slide outline. Each line names the slide's role in the argument.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.what: Add a short glossary of the terms that recur: one name per concept, a one-line definition and the names to avoid.

steps.title: Approval
steps.what: Ask the user to approve the outline and the key terms. Build nothing until they do.
